data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because any action-guiding choice necessarily assumes the future will resemble the past, which Popper explicitly forbade as a logical principle.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent admits they are acting on a blind guess and the preference is merely psychological comfort, the charge of smuggling induction fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'preference' is redefined strictly as 'choosing the best target for attempted falsification' rather than 'choosing the best basis for action', the inductive step is avoided.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If one accepts that rational action does not require probable truth, only the absence of known falsity, the inductive gap is bridged without induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"To 'prefer' theory A over theory B for action (e.g., building a bridge) implies an expectation that A will not fail where B might. This expectation relies on the assumption that the conditions which allowed A to survive past tests will persist. Since Popper denies that survival increases probability, the only ground for this expectation is the uniformity of nature (induction). Without this hidden premise, the preference is arbitrary; with it, Popper's system collapses into the very inductivism he sought to replace.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
